analysis.one_liner: Raises the government's burden of proof in civil asset forfeiture cases and stops police from keeping the proceeds.
analysis.headline: The FAIR Act died in the Senate Judiciary Committee after its January 2015 introduction; the record shows only two actions—introduction and referral—and no hearing, markup, or vote ever took place.
analysis.plain_summary: Civil asset forfeiture lets the government take cash, cars, homes, and bank accounts from people who have not been charged with a crime, based on suspicion the property was tied to an offense—and the owner must fight to get it back. This bill would have made the government prove its case with clear and convincing evidence, required proof that the owner actually knew about or helped the alleged offense, guaranteed owners a lawyer, expanded judges' power to reject seizures wildly out of proportion to the offense, and forced courts to promptly return money seized from bank accounts for 'structuring' deposits. Its most structural change: forfeited property and proceeds would go to the Treasury's General Fund instead of back into law enforcement budgets, removing the financial incentive agencies currently have to seize first and ask questions later.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who own property—especially cash-earning small business owners, drivers whose cash is taken during traffic stops, and account holders whose banks are seized by the IRS for deposit patterns—because they would get a lawyer, a tougher government burden of proof, a hearing within 14 days for seized monetary instruments, and proportionality review that considers hardship to the family.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the government's burden of proof in civil forfeiture from a mere preponderance of the evidence to clear and convincing evidence [S2] [S3].

Requires the government to show that the property owner used the property to commit an offense, or knowingly consented or was willfully blind to its use—not merely that the property was connected to some offense [S2] [S3].
Ensures every person contesting a civil forfeiture has legal representation, without the current exception for owners whose property is their primary residence [S2] [S3].
Directs forfeited proceeds to the Treasury General Fund instead of Department of Justice accounts, removing the profit motive for agencies that keep what they seize [S2] [S3].

Adds a knowing-intent requirement to the structuring prohibition and requires a court hearing within 14 days to return seized bank accounts unless the government shows probable cause—protections aimed at IRS seizures of small business owners' deposits [S2] [S3].
Expands the proportionality factors courts must weigh, including the seriousness of the offense, the property's value, and hardship to the owner and dependents [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies—federal and state and local police departments that currently receive forfeited cash, vehicles, and property as funding—would lose a revenue stream they treat as a budget supplement, and prosecutors would face a higher standard of proof in forfeiture cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police agencies funded by seized property

drawbacks.text: Prosecutors and police argue that a lower proof standard and looser property nexus rules are needed to strip assets from drug trafficking organizations, and that raising the burden to clear and convincing evidence would make it harder to dismantle them.

Routing proceeds to the General Fund eliminates dedicated forfeiture revenues that currently fund law enforcement operations and some victim-related programs, forcing those costs back onto appropriated budgets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits fall on a large group of property owners who today must prove their own innocence to recover seized homes, cash, and accounts; the costs fall on law enforcement budgets and on cases against traffickers, which is the strongest good-faith objection. The bill also tightens the structuring rules at the same time it protects innocent account holders, so it does not simply open the door to money laundering.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or markup, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the FAIR Act on January 26, 2015 [S1] [S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day; the action history shows no further action through the end of the 114th Congress [S5].
Five senators cosponsored it—two Republicans, one Independent, and two Democrats [S4].

The CRS summary confirms the bill's core reforms: a clear-and-convincing evidence standard, owner-knowledge requirements, guaranteed legal representation, proportionality review, and deposit of proceeds into the Treasury General Fund [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies that rely on forfeiture proceeds kept their funding stream, and property owners remained subject to seizure under the old lower-proof rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies that profit from seizures

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Act in the Senate and framed it as restoring Fifth Amendment property rights.

for.name: Five Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors across party lines, the only recorded support the bill drew during the Congress.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral ( chaired by a Republican in the 114th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it in two years.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's recorded support crossed party lines—five cosponsors split 2 Republicans, 1 Independent, 2 Democrats—and no floor vote or recorded opposition ever occurred; the bill simply never moved out of committee.

industries.industry: Federal and state/local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: These agencies currently receive forfeited cash, vehicles, and proceeds directly into their own accounts, so their budgets depend partly on what they seize from civilians. The bill would have routed proceeds to the Treasury General Fund, ending that self-funding loop [S2] [S3].

The bill raises the government's proof standard and adds owner-knowledge requirements, making forfeiture cases harder to win; groups that defend forfeiture as an anti-cartel tool had an interest in the bill stalling, and no committee action ever occurred [S2] [S5].
